segments.text: Industrial-organizational psychology applies psychological knowledge to work. It studies how people are selected, motivated, led, socialized and supported in organizations, and how organizational systems affect behaviour and performance.
Aspirants often find this unit easy because every concept can be linked with a workplace example. The key is to remain analytical rather than giving management slogans.

items.text: Leadership styles

: Leadership can be studied through traits, behaviour, situation and relationships. Autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire are simple style labels, but modern answers should also note that effectiveness depends on context.
Decision making

: Work decisions can be affected by limited information, time pressure, biases, group processes and organizational rules. Good decision systems try to improve information quality and reduce avoidable bias.
Work motivation
: Apply motivation theories to goals, rewards, fairness, autonomy, meaning and expectations at work. Different employees may respond differently to the same incentive.
Organizational culture
: Organizational culture refers to shared assumptions, values and practices that shape “how things are done.” It is learned through leadership, stories, routines, rewards and socialization.
Stress and conflict

: Workload, role ambiguity, low control, interpersonal conflict and poor support can contribute to stress. Management may involve job design, communication, support, conflict-resolution systems and individual coping resources.
Organizational socialization
: New members learn the norms, roles and expectations of the workplace through orientation, observation, mentoring and experience.
Job-related attitudes
: Job satisfaction, organizational commitment and engagement are attitudes or states linked with work experience, but they are not identical concepts.
Sexual harassment and glass ceiling

: Sexual harassment concerns unwanted sex-based conduct in work contexts and should be treated as an ethical, legal and organizational issue. The glass ceiling describes invisible structural barriers that can limit advancement of qualified people, especially women, into higher positions.
Human-computer interaction
: HCI studies how people interact with technology. Good design considers attention, memory, error prevention, workload, usability and accessibility.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

blocks.text: Industrial and organizational sides of the field

items.text: Industrial/personnel psychology
: Focuses on job analysis, recruitment, selection, performance measurement and training. The central question is how to make decisions about people using valid, fair and job-related evidence.
Organizational psychology
: Focuses on motivation, leadership, teams, culture, attitudes, stress and organizational change. It examines both individual experience and the systems that shape behaviour.
Job analysis
: Job analysis identifies tasks, responsibilities and required knowledge, skills and abilities. It provides a defensible foundation for selection, training and performance criteria.
Predictors

: Organizations may use structured interviews, work samples, cognitive measures or other tools. Predictors should be selected because evidence shows relevance to job performance, not because they appear impressive.
Criterion problem
: Performance is multidimensional. Task performance, citizenship behaviour, safety, creativity and counterproductive behaviour are not identical, so a single rating may be incomplete.
Structured interviews
: Using standardized job-related questions and anchored scoring generally improves reliability compared with informal conversational interviews.
Fairness
: Selection systems should be monitored for job relevance, accessibility and adverse effects. A technically reliable measure can still be inappropriate if it creates construct-irrelevant barriers.
Expectancy
: Employees are more likely to exert effort when they believe effort can produce performance, performance can produce valued outcomes and the outcomes matter to them.
Equity/fairness
: Perceived fairness concerns both outcomes and procedures. A reward can lose motivational value if allocation is experienced as arbitrary or disrespectful.
Goal setting
: Specific, challenging but attainable goals can improve performance when people accept the goal and receive feedback. Goals can also narrow attention, so quality and ethical safeguards matter.
Job characteristics

: Skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback can affect meaningfulness and motivation. Job redesign can therefore be a system-level intervention rather than placing all responsibility on the worker.
Trait and behavioural approaches
: Leadership research identifies personal characteristics and behaviours associated with effective influence, but no single trait guarantees effectiveness across every situation.
Contingency approaches
: Fiedler and later contingency theories emphasize fit between leadership style and situational demands. The practical lesson is that context, task structure and follower needs matter.
Transformational leadership

: Transformational models emphasize vision, intellectual stimulation and individualized consideration. Positive associations are common, but leadership outcomes also depend on organizational systems and should not be reduced to charisma.
Decision bias
: Confirmation bias, overconfidence, availability and group pressures can distort decisions. Structured decision procedures, independent estimates and dissent can reduce some errors.

blocks.text: Culture, socialization, stress and contemporary work

items.text: Culture

: Organizational culture is reproduced through recruitment, leadership behaviour, reward systems, stories, routines and informal norms. Stated values matter less when incentives reward contradictory behaviour.
Socialization

: Newcomers learn technical tasks and social expectations through orientation, observation, mentoring and feedback. Effective socialization reduces uncertainty without requiring uncritical conformity.
Work stress

: Stress can arise from excessive demands, low control, role conflict, insecurity, harassment or poor support. Individual coping can help, but prevention often requires workload, staffing, leadership or job-design changes.
Sexual harassment

: Harassment is not merely interpersonal discomfort; it is an organizational and legal issue involving unwanted sex-based conduct and power. Prevention requires clear policy, reporting pathways, accountability and a climate in which retaliation is not tolerated.
Glass ceiling

: The glass-ceiling concept describes structural barriers that restrict advancement despite apparent formal equality. Analysis should examine promotion criteria, networks, caregiving penalties, stereotypes and access to developmental assignments.
Human-computer interaction

: HCI applies knowledge of perception, attention, memory and error to technology design. Systems should make important information visible, prevent predictable mistakes, reduce unnecessary cognitive load and support accessibility.
Attach one workplace example to every concept.
Make a leadership comparison but also write “appropriate style depends on task, people and context.”
Prepare stress as causes → effects → individual measures → organizational measures.
Use HCI examples such as form design, dashboards or warning systems.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define I/O psychology, organize the answer into leadership/decisions, motivation/culture, stress/conflict, socialization/attitudes and contemporary workplace issues.
• Work behaviour is shaped by both person and organization.
• Organizational culture is learned and reinforced through practices.
• Stress management is not only an individual responsibility; job and organizational design matter too.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
